articles.title: Read your way there

body.support:
Planning a trip is a reading job.

1. **Use a planner.** The Transport Victoria app, or Google Maps. Type where you're going and **when you need to get there**.
2. **Skim the options.** Pick one that gets you there **on time** with the **fewest changes**.
3. **Scan the details.** Find the **time**, the **stop**, the **platform** and the **direction**.
4. **Check for changes.** Only look at **your line** and **your day**.
5. **Write the steps down.** *Walk to stop 12. Catch the 901 at 8:14.* Then a flat phone won't stop you.

Under 18? Travel is **free** with a **Youth myki**. Still **touch on**.
body.core:
Planning a trip on public transport is a reading job. Here's how to do it fast.

1. **Ask the planner.** Use the Transport Victoria app or website (or Google Maps). Type **where from**, **where to** and **when you need to arrive**, not just when you'll leave.
2. **Skim the options.** You'll get a list. Skim for the ones that get you there **on time**, with the **fewest changes** and the least walking.
3. **Scan the details.** Open your pick and scan for the exact **times**, **stop numbers**, **platforms** and **direction** (*towards City* or *towards Frankston*). One wrong direction can cost you an hour.
4. **Check for disruptions.** Works and problems are listed as **service changes**. Most won't matter. Look only for **your line**, **your day** and **your time**.
5. **Write it down as steps.** *Walk to stop 12. Catch the 901 at 8:14. Get off at the station.* If your phone dies, you can still get there.

Under 18? You travel **free** with a **Youth myki**. You still need to **touch on**.
body.extend:
Planning a trip on public transport is a series of reading decisions.

1. **Query the planner.** In the Transport Victoria app or website (or Google Maps), set origin, destination and **arrival time**. Planning backwards from when you must arrive builds in a buffer.
2. **Skim for relevance.** The planner returns several options. Skim them against your criteria: arrival time, number of transfers, walking distance and cost or accessibility needs.
3. **Scan for precise details.** Times, stop numbers, platforms and **direction of travel** are where errors happen. Check each one.
4. **Filter disruptions.** Service-change notices are long and mostly irrelevant to you. Decide what's relevant by line, date and time, then read those notices in full.
5. **Summarise as sequential steps.** Paraphrasing the plan into short instructions (*Walk to stop 12; catch the 901 at 8:14*) makes it portable and checkable, and works when your battery doesn't.

Since 1 January 2026, under-18s travel free with a **Youth myki**, but still need to touch on.

caseStudies.title: Free travel for under-18s

body.support:
On **1 January 2026**, Victoria made public transport **free for under-18s**. Trains, trams and buses, every day, all over the state.

You need a **Youth myki**. It costs **$5**. You can buy it online or at a station with staff. It works until you turn 18.

This helps young people get to school, TAFE, work and sport without a lift. But you still need to read the app and the timetable.
body.core:
On **1 January 2026**, the Victorian Government made public transport **free for everyone under 18**, every day, on trains, trams and buses across the state.

To use it, young people need a **Youth myki**. It costs **$5** and can be bought online on the Transport Victoria website or at staffed stations. It stays valid until you turn 18.

It works on metro and regional services. On booked V/Line trips, you use the card number. On regional buses that don't use myki, you show the card.

The change matters for young people getting to school, TAFE, work and sport without a lift. But free travel only helps if you can read the planner, the timetable and the service changes.
body.extend:
From **1 January 2026**, the Victorian Government made public transport **free for everyone under 18**, every day, on trains, trams and buses across the state.

You need a **Youth myki**. It costs **$5** online through Transport Victoria or at staffed stations, and it works until you turn 18. It covers city and country services. For booked V/Line trips you use the card number. On country buses that don't take myki, you show the card.

The change removes cost as a barrier to getting to school, work and sport. But it doesn't remove the reading barrier. Reading journey planners, timetables and notices about changes is what turns free travel into real independence.

teacher.answers:
**Journey plan:** 1 arrive-by time; 2 summary (leave, duration, changes); 3 walk to stop 12; 4 bus 901 towards Station; 5 train, platform 2, towards City; 6 weekend-only service change (not relevant on Tuesday).

**Sort:** weekend buses replace trains — doesn't; stop 12 closed Tue–Thu — affects; tram 86 — doesn't; trains towards City delays 7–9 am — affects; lift out of order — doesn't (unless you need it); bus 903 holidays — doesn't.

**Case study:** under-18s, from 1 January 2026, statewide; Youth myki, $5, online (Transport Victoria) or staffed stations; valid until 18.

realityCheck: **Rural and regional students** may have few services. The skills still apply (V/Line, regional buses, school buses), but pick realistic destinations, and expect “there's no bus” to be a real answer worth discussing.

**Doing the trip is the best part — and the hardest to organise.** An excursion needs permission and supervision. If you can't, the planning alone still meets the learning goals; ask students to do it with family.
**Some students already travel independently;** others never have. Pair them up: experienced travellers make great guides.
**Check the details.** Youth myki rules, prices and the website name may change. Check Transport Victoria the week you teach.
**Accessibility:** for students with disability or anxiety about travel, include lift and accessibility info in the planning, and don't force a trip.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's very concrete, and the free-travel change makes it immediately useful for VPC students.
